caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.638 of 2004
lawyer:
For Petitioners: Mr. Subhash Chandra Saha, Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-oh-Record
For Respondents: Not represented.
parties:
Md. Serajul Islam & another ------ Petitioners
Versus
Md. Abdul Latif & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. M. M. Ruhul Amin, J:- This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 05.01.2004 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 1444 of 2004 summarily rejecting the application. 

2. Short facts are that the pre-emptor filed Pre-emption Case No.41 of 1991 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Pirganj, Rangpur under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-emption against the preemptees and others stating, inter alia, that the land measuring 66 decimals of Plot No.381/628 of C,S. Khatian No.2, S.A. Khatian No.115 originally belonged to Naresh Chanara Basu and Indu Prava Basu in their raiyati right. The C.S. Khatian was accordingly prepared and finally published in their names. Before R.S. Khatian the said Naresh Chandra Basu and Indu Prava Basu after transferring the said land including the case land left for India. Md. Akbar Ali, Munsur Ali, Hosen Ali and Hosen Ali got the case land on the basis of lease. As per the deed of exchange dated 27.12.1986 Md. Akbar Ali transferred 161/2 acres of land to the pre-emptor. In this way the preemptor became a co-sharer in the disputed holding. The pre-emptor has got his homestead in the western portion of the case land. The opposite party No.3 of the pm-emption case sold the case land to the pre-emptee Nos.1 and 2 by a kabala dated 03.04.1991 beyond the knowledge of the preemptor. No notice of the kabala under pre-emption was served upon the pre-emptor. The pre-emptees are stranger purchasers in the case holding. The cause of action of the .case arose when the kabala under pre-emption was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act. 

3. The pre-emptees contested the case by filing written objection stating, inter alia, that the case is not maintainable in its present form and manner. It is barred by the Land Reforms Ordinance, 1984. The pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case holding. The pre-emptees have homestead in the case land and they have no other land except the case land to construct their homestead and have been living therein. The pre-emptees spent Tk.1,000/- by cutting mud in the southern portion of the case land for making a bhiti for constructing a dwelling but by spending Tk.2000/- and spent of Tk.200/- for constructing a cow shed and also constructed a bamboo fence at a cost of Tk.500/-. The pre-emptee No:2 also spent Tk. I 000/- for constructing a dwelling but in the northern portion of the case land. So the pre-emption case is liable to fail. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge, Pirganj Rangpur upon hearing the learned Advocates for the parties and consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties allowed the pre-emption case. The pre-emptees preferred appeal and the appellate court allowed the appeal in part and modified the judgment of the trial court to the effect that pre-emptor would pay Tk.4000/- to the pre-emptees as cost of improvement. 

5. The pre-emptor moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction against the order of cost of improvement and obtained Rule. The High Court Division upon hearing the learned Advocates for the parties and consideration of the materials on record rejected the revisional application summarily. 

6. We have heard Mr. Subhash Chandra Saha, the learned Counsel for the petitioners and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers. 

7. It appears that the trial court and the appellate court concurrently held that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by way of exchange in the case holding and the pre-emptees are stranger purchasers and the pre-emption application was within time and also not bad for defect of party. The pre-emptees did not take any exception against the above concurrent findings of the trial court and the appellate court. 

8. It appears that the trial court allowed Tk.1200/- as improvement of cost whereas the appellate court allowed Tk.4,000/- as cost of improvement and the pre-emptor moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction against the cost of improvement of Tk.4000/- as awarded by the appellate court. 

9. Mr. Saha submitted that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer. In our view this argument of the learned Advocate cannot be accepted as it is the concurrent finding of the trial court and the appellate court that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer and the pre-emptees are stranger purchasers. Mr. Saha next argued that under section. 6 of Land Reform Ordinance, 1984. the pre-emption case is barred. 

10. The High Court Division held that the provisions of section 6 of the Ordinance, 1984 are not attracted in the pre-emption case and the pre-emption case is quite maintainable. 

11. For ready reference let us reproduce below section 6 of Land Reform Ordinance. 1984: 
"Any land used as homestead by its owner in the rural area shall be exempted from all legal processes, including seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any officer, Court or any other authority and the owner of such land shall not be divested or dispossessed of the land or evicted there from by any means; Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to the acquisition of such homestead under any law." On perusal of section 6 of the Ordinance, we are of the view that if section 6 is read with the proviso it lands to the conclusion that the same is not attract in a pre-emption proceeding. 

12. In the circumstances, we find no substances in the submissions of the learned Counsel. 

13. Accordingly, the petition is dismissed. 

End.
